query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Microalloying the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with trace amounts of yttrium (Y) and hafnium (Hf) will improve its performance under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room‐temperature creep, and corrosive environments.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA with a uniform fine lamellar structure that presently provides good strength and plasticity but limited high‐temperature and corrosion performance.
generation.intervention: Incorporate minor amounts of Y and Hf into the alloy composition during processing.
generation.conditions: Test under service-relevant conditions such as cyclic high-temperature exposure (e.g., around 900 °C), long-term mechanical loading (creep conditions), and exposure to corrosive environments (e.g., molten salt media simulating hot corrosion), similar to those expected for aircraft and spacecraft fasteners.
generation.structural_mediator: Segregation of Y and Hf to grain boundaries and surfaces, promoting the in situ formation of a continuous and thermally stable oxide layer as well as enhanced grain-boundary cohesion.
generation.mechanism: During processing and subsequent high-temperature exposure, the microalloying elements (Y and Hf) are expected to preferentially segregate at grain boundaries. This segregation promotes the formation of adherent, stable oxides that inhibit grain-boundary sliding (thereby reducing creep) and suppress grain coarsening, while also providing a barrier against corrosive attack, thus maintaining the alloy’s fine lamellar structure and enabling high strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: The YHf-doped alloy will exhibit lower creep rates, improved retention of strength and ductility at elevated temperatures, and reduced corrosion damage (e.g., lower oxide scale spallation) relative to the base AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy.
generation.baseline: Performance of the unmodified AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA, which, despite its fine lamellar structure, falls short of meeting industrial requirements for long-term thermal stability, creep resistance, and corrosion resistance.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected to be effective in single-phase alloys produced by standard industrial methods (e.g., casting or laser cladding) under the specific range of high-temperature and corrosive conditions; effects outside these regimes (such as extremely low temperatures or radically different processing routes) remain to be verified.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal concentration of Y and Hf and their exact segregation behavior under cyclic thermal and mechanical loading are not fully determined, and long-term stability under actual service conditions needs further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, one modified with a trace addition of Y and Hf and one as the control. Process both sets under identical conditions. Subject the samples to cyclic high-temperature tests (e.g., 900 °C with thermal cycling), prolonged creep tests under controlled stress, and hot corrosion tests in molten salt environments that simulate operational aggressors.
measurements: Measure yield strength, ductility, and hardness at room and elevated temperatures via tensile testing and nanoindentation.
Quantify creep rates under long-term loading conditions.
Assess oxide scale formation, adhesion, and spallation via microscopy (e.g., SEM/TEM) and surface analysis techniques.
Perform microstructural characterization to verify grain boundary segregation of Y and Hf.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the YHf-doped samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in creep resistance, maintenance of fine lamellar microstructure, and corrosion/oxidation behavior (i.e., similar oxide scale spallation and mechanical performance to the control alloy) under the test conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractBoth crack-free AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) and Y and Hf co-doping AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA (YHf-EHEA) coatings were prepared by laser cladding. The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. The experimental results showed that the structure of the as-deposited coatings consisted of FCC and BCC/B2 phases. After heat treatment, an Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC phase of all coatings. The grain sizes of the EHEA and YHf-EHEA coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Meanwhile, after hot corrosion, the spallation areas of the YHf-EHEA and EHEA coatings accounted for 14.98% and 5.67% of the total surface area, respectively.
